short: Nigeria has no AI statute. The National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, 2025 contains a binding AI chapter enforced by NITDA; meanwhile the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 binds, with fines of up to 2% of annual gross revenue.
title: Nigeria AI Laws
subtitle: An AI chapter in the Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, and the Data Protection Act that binds
body_html:
Status at a glance

AI bill pending. Nigeria has no AI statute. The National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, 2025, before the National Assembly, contains a binding chapter on artificial intelligence (ss. 63 to 69) that would make the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) the AI regulator. Until it is enacted, AI that processes personal data is governed by the Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023, whose section 37 gives a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions. Verified on 25 October 2026 against the National Assembly, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and NITDA.

Key instruments

InstrumentNumberDateStatus
National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, 2025National Assembly bill document 11219 (Senate, 10th Assembly)2025Not enacted
Nigeria Data Protection Act, 20232023 No. 37Commencement 12 June 2023In force
National Artificial Intelligence StrategyNCAIR/NITDA draft2024Draft policy

Who regulates and enforces

  • National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA): the regulatory agency for AI under the bill (ss. 66 to 68).
  • Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC): enforces the Data Protection Act, including section 37 on automated decisions.

Scope and reach

The bill would reach any person or public institution that develops, deploys or uses an AI system (s. 63), and "artificial intelligence agents" (s. 2). The Data Protection Act already reaches controllers and processors outside Nigeria that process the personal data of a data subject in Nigeria (s. 2(2)(c)).

Core obligations

  • Under the bill, if enacted: AI must be fair, transparent and explainable, safe, accountable, contestable, under human oversight and compliant with the Data Protection Act (s. 63(1)); risk-proportionate governance and impact assessment, user information, bias safeguards, audit records and disclosure of the operator's identity (s. 64(1)); risk classification by NITDA regulation (s. 65); an annual system impact assessment report (s. 69).
  • Today: the Data Protection Act, including the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions, with human intervention and a right to contest (s. 37).

Penalties

BreachMaximumProvisionEnforcer
Data Protection Act infringements by a controller or processor of major importanceThe greater of NGN 10,000,000 and 2% of annual gross revenue in the preceding financial yearNDPA s. 48(4)NDPC
Other Data Protection Act infringementsThe greater of NGN 2,000,000 and 2% of annual gross revenueNDPA s. 48(5)NDPC
An AI agent violating the bill or its regulations, if enactedThe higher of 10,000,000 (no currency is stated in the text) and 2% of annual gross revenue from NigeriaBill s. 68(2)(d)NITDA

What is coming next

  • The bill's remaining stages and presidential assent; no official date was found, and the National Assembly's bill tracker does not show the stage.

The bill's passage, the other bills, and the strategy

The bill's progress has outrun every forecast. The Senate and House ICT committees held a joint public hearing on 10 November 2025 at which the Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Bosun Tijani, said the President would assent within the week; Bloomberg reported on 13 January 2026 that passage was targeted for the end of March 2026, with NITDA's director general saying Nigeria would be among the first African countries with an economy-wide AI framework; Tech Hive Advisory then expected enactment in the second quarter of 2026. The press reported a third reading in July 2026, as the earlier note on this page records. No gazetted Act and no assent notice was found when this page was checked on 4 November 2026, so the bill is still treated as pending. As summarised by Bloomberg and BusinessDay, the AI chapter would let NITDA classify AI systems by risk, require licensing for high-risk systems, mandate algorithmic transparency, accredit AI auditors, demand information from AI providers and issue enforcement directives, with penalties reported as up to 2% of annual gross revenue; it would also require AI operators to cooperate with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, creating a dual regime with the NDPA.

It is not the only AI bill. The National Artificial Intelligence Commission (Establishment) Bill, 2025 (SB 731), introduced in the Senate in February 2025 and read in May, would create a standalone AI commission; the Nigerian Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2025 (HB 2567), introduced in the House in October 2025, would set an ethics and governance framework; the Copyright Act (Amendment) Bill, 2025 (HB 2559) would make unauthorised commercial use of an AI-generated digital replica an infringement; and a Nigeria Digital Sovereignty and Fair Data Compensation Bill, 2025 would pay Nigerians for the use of their data. Two 2023 bills on AI and robotics passed first reading and lapsed. Whichever bill passes first, NITDA and the NDPC are the regulators it names.

The National AI Strategy, drafted in 2024, was published in final form by the ministry in September 2025 with objectives and implementation priorities for 2025 to 2029, including national AI principles and an AI governance body. On the data side, the NDPC's General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) of 2025 turned the NDPA into operating rules, and the Commission announced plans for regulatory AI sandboxes, so a company deploying AI with Nigerian personal data already answers to the NDPC under section 37 and the GAID while the AI bill waits.

Last verified

4 November 2026, against the sources above. The bill's AI chapter as summarised, the penalty figure, the other 2025 bills and the September 2025 strategy publication are as Bloomberg, BusinessDay, Digital Policy Alert and Tech Hive report them, not read on the National Assembly's site, and are reported rather than verified. Not confirmed on an official source: whether the bill has passed third reading or received assent.
